title: How Business AI Use is Changing
dek: Three fresh enterprise AI datasets from Ramp, Databricks and Arcana Research point the same way: price competition has handed buyers real leverage, and the leading companies are using a lot more AI without paying proportionally more for it. Plus: Nvidia's board appears to shut the door on Jensen's return, Commerce finally moves on chip diversion, and OpenAI's embedded safety evaluators fall short of what was promised.

oneIdea.headline: Business AI has become a buyer's market, and the smart buyers are using it.
oneIdea.summary: Across Ramp, Databricks and Arcana Research, the convergent story is stronger than the divergent one. Model competition is pushing token prices down, enterprises are switching and mixing providers far more readily, and the leaders are growing usage much faster than spend. The open question is whether the top 1% of spenders, at hundreds of times the median, are outliers or a preview of where everyone else is heading. That answer will shape the size of the market and whether all this CapEx turns into ROI. For enterprises themselves, the practical takeaway is that you probably have more negotiating leverage than you are using, as long as you've built the infrastructure to switch.

gpCorner.note: AI commentary for UK general practice; not from the podcast

items.title: Token prices fell a fifth; has your scribe price moved?
items.body: The average price suppliers pay the two main labs fell 21 per cent in October. Scribe and triage vendors buy those tokens. NLW's advice to businesses applies to a practice or PCN: you probably have more leverage than you are using. At renewal, ask whether lower model costs are being passed on. Zitron would say the cuts show sellers under strain, which is a reason to keep contracts short.

items.title: Leverage depends on being able to leave
items.body: The buyers getting deals are those who can switch. In general practice that means data portability: can consultation notes, templates and audit logs be exported in a usable form, and does the tool sit on top of the clinical system or lock into it. Ask before signing, not at renewal.

items.title: Independent auditors chosen by the audited
items.body: OpenAI has let outside safety evaluators in, but chooses them and controls what they see; one evaluator said the access does not meet its own bar. The parallel in health is familiar. We would not accept a manufacturer selecting and briefing its own inspector. DTAC and clinical safety sign-off should rest on evidence a supplier cannot curate.

the_other_side.text: Zitron, writing the same day, reads the concentration of spending as weakness, not a preview. He says about 80 per cent of OpenAI's and Anthropic's revenue comes from one per cent of their customers, most of them unprofitable AI start-ups, several funded by Nvidia. He cites the same source Whittemore uses, Ramp, as showing Anthropic's growth slowing to 15 to 25 per cent a quarter from 47 per cent, and asks how those customers will afford tokens once funding tightens. His summary is that "the vast majority of people do not want to pay for AI". He does not discuss falling token prices or switching between providers.

the_truth_beneath.text: The variable both men orbit is whether the heaviest one per cent of AI spenders are the future or the whole market. Both accept as fact that spending is extremely concentrated, that Ramp's data show spend growth slowing, and that engineering teams account for most of it. The empirical question is whether the median company's spending rises towards the top; the observable is the median spend per employee in Ramp's index over the next year, now about sixteen dollars a month. The residue is worldview: whether flat spending with rising use shows a healthy buyer's market or sellers cutting prices to hold customers. For Whittemore to be vindicated, median spend must climb while prices fall and use spreads beyond coding. For Zitron, the top spenders must cut back as venture money tightens, with the median unmoved. Both are polemicists with incentives: Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype. The signal is that both say spend growth has slowed sharply. Watch Ramp's median figure.

headlines.headline: Nvidia's board throws cold water on a Jensen comeback
headlines.summary: A 180,000-signature petition, shareholder letters from Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker, and even President Trump ("That certainly isn't a bad idea") backed Jensen's return. On Monday, sources told CNBC the board is focused on Wachtell Lipton's independent investigation into whether his conduct compromised national security or company secrets, and is not discussing bringing him back.

headlines.headline: The revenues and demand are growing so strongly that I think the industry will be fine.
headlines.attribution: Sam Altman, at Semafor's event, on AI without Jensen Huang
headlines.summary: Altman's answer to fears about losing Nvidia as AI's de facto central bank. Even OpenAI relied on a $100 billion Nvidia guarantee for its Ohio facility, but he insists "people still trust their guarantees very much."

headlines.headline: I don't even need you guys. I could just give all this capacity to Elon.
headlines.attribution: Jensen Huang, to NeoCloud executives at a Berlin meeting last month, as reported by The Wall Street Journal
headlines.summary: Per The Wall Street Journal, Jensen was already pulling back on commitments and demanding upfront payment from NeoCloud bosses before his resignation. Interim CEO Colette Kress is expected to rein in data center backstops further, and Needham warns of a more uncertain credit environment for NeoClouds.

headlines.headline: Commerce finally moves to close the chip diversion loophole
headlines.summary: A long-awaited rule targets Chinese labs reaching Nvidia chips through third-party countries. Data center operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil now need export licenses for advanced AI chips, and existing facilities have 90 days to get them, which lets Commerce investigate prior shipments.

headlines.headline: The administration's chip-policy feud spills into public
headlines.summary: The new rule says it was written "by and at the direction of" Treasury and the NSC. Sources say Bessent pushed it through with Rubio's support. Trump framed the split as one secretary who wants to be friendly with China and one who wants a blowup. A former Commerce official couldn't recall another agency distancing itself from its own rule, and warns the visible infighting invites workarounds.

headlines.headline: Nvidia, OpenAI and Anthropic set to be named 'national champions'
headlines.summary: Commerce is expected to name its first AI national champions next week: reportedly Nvidia, Amazon, Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic. The designation brings expedited export licenses, government help with international business development, and federal financing. A core goal is bundling chips, models and products for international sales.

headlines.headline: OpenAI lets safety evaluators inside, with strings attached
headlines.summary: Apollo Research, METR, Transluce and Goodfire get "deep access" to internal models. Apollo's six-person team will spend four months testing whether models subvert alignment and control mechanisms. But OpenAI can withhold information, limit staff access, keep evaluators off Slack, and censor reports for confidential details. Conclusions must still be published unchanged.

headlines.headline: Its access and disclosure rights don't yet meet our bar for full embedded evaluations.
headlines.attribution: Apollo Research, on its embedded evaluation agreement with OpenAI
headlines.summary: The evaluator itself called the pilot only "an ambitious first step." DeepMind's Neel Nanda said it falls short of the employee-like access Altman promised in September, and ex-OpenAI researcher Steven Adler criticized what he called a "tattletale clause" routing employee concerns through OpenAI.

headlines.headline: Handpicked auditors aren't independent auditors
headlines.summary: Even if Anthropic's version is better, labs are still choosing their own evaluators and deciding what access they get. That's reasonable for a business, but its incentives differ from the societal need auditors are supposed to serve. Embedded independent auditing is one of the rare safety ideas with broad consensus, so it deserves agreed-upon standards set by a genuinely independent force.

headlines.headline: A banking outage deepens the 'something doesn't add up' mood
headlines.summary: Logins, ATMs and transfers failed across JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, Zelle and more, traced back to Chase's backend systems. Chase blamed a software bug in on-premises hardware, not a cyberattack. After Microsoft and FAA outages, public sentiment is growing more incredulous of the denials, and AI's role in that narrative is one to watch.

headlines.headline: Businesses used 36% more tokens and paid just 2% more
headlines.summary: Ramp's latest index shows total token consumption across its businesses up more than a third in a month while spend barely moved. Usage growth is now clearly outpacing spend growth.

headlines.headline: Cheaper models are forcing everyone's prices down
headlines.summary: Average price per million tokens across OpenAI and Anthropic fell 21% in October. That doesn't necessarily mean companies are moving to cheaper Chinese models. The mere presence of those models is pressuring the big providers, on top of their own push toward more efficient models.

headlines.headline: Single-provider enterprises went from majority to minority in four months
headlines.summary: In July, 64% of companies on Databricks' Unity Gateway used one model provider. By early November, 72% used two or more. Databricks argues raw token price is the wrong number to watch, and that the metric that matters is cost per successful task.

headlines.headline: AI is an eight-figure budget line, and most leaders can't see it
headlines.summary: Arcana's Global 2000 survey finds 91% expect to spend more on AI in 2026, mostly 20-40% more. Yet two-thirds lack visibility into their model and API spend. That's a sign of the gap between vanguard companies and the middle of the pack, and likely something that changes fast.

headlines.headline: A third of OpenAI customers are open to switching
headlines.summary: In Arcana's survey, a third of OpenAI customers said they'd consider moving, frequently to Anthropic. 43% of GitHub Copilot customers were open to switching, generally naming Claude Code. Switching is becoming normal, and that is what gives buyers leverage.

headlines.headline: The top 1% of AI spenders are in a different universe
headlines.summary: On Ramp, the median firm spends $16.32 per employee per month, while top firms spend over $10,000, about 625 times as much. Ramp skews tech-forward, but Databricks sees the same pattern: a $2.49 median user against a 99th percentile of nearly $700 a week, a 281x gap.

headlines.headline: Coding remains king
headlines.summary: 72% of AI spend on Ramp comes from engineering teams. A third of Arcana's Global 2000 respondents are piloting AI coding tools, the largest pilot group of any category.

headlines.headline: Anthropic has the enterprise momentum on every scoreboard
headlines.summary: Just under 45% of US businesses on Ramp pay Anthropic, versus 40.6% for OpenAI. Anthropic takes 68.8% of proprietary model tokens on Unity Gateway, and 81% of Arcana respondents named it when asked for an exciting AI vendor.

headlines.headline: Customer service is AI's fastest-growing business use case
headlines.summary: Customer support teams' share of AI spend on Ramp jumped from 0.8% in June to 13.3% in November. 38% of Arcana's Global 2000 respondents already use AI customer service.

headlines.headline: Spend growth has slowed, but it still lands in the forecast range
headlines.summary: Ramp token spend grew 1.05% in August, 0.22% in September and 1.65% in October. If October's rate held, it would compound to about 22% a year. That's a real slowdown from past growth, but still within the 20-40% increase Arcana's respondents expect.

headlines.headline: Opus 5.5 may be crowding out Fable
headlines.summary: Frontier models' share of Ramp spend rose from 67.7% to 69.5% in October, yet Fable's token share on Databricks fell from 5.5% to 0.6%. Over six weeks, Opus 5.5 climbed from 7.2% to 37.9% of Databricks tokens. The divergence may be less about frontier models in general than Opus simply leaving Fable 5.2 without a place.

headlines.headline: 2026 was the year agents got real, just not for the average enterprise
headlines.summary: Year-end retrospectives will likely crown 2026 the year of agents. Yet Arcana ranks autonomous agents fourth on its heat index of what companies are excited about, and dead last on its adoption index of what's actually deployed.

headlines.headline: The market question: are the 1% outliers or a preview?
headlines.summary: Each dataset has caveats: gateway-only customers, a narrow tech-forward sample, a small Global 2000 pool. But the convergent story outweighs the divergent one. The big question is how far the median buyer drifts toward the 1% spending hundreds of times more. That will say a lot about market size and whether the CapEx turns into ROI.

headlines.headline: You probably have more leverage than you're using
headlines.summary: Competition is vicious, and model providers are desperate not to become generic commodities. There are deals to be had, but only if you've built the infrastructure to actually switch.
